question: On 9/28/76, the HUD Secretary (at the time) made a speech to the Ft Worth Federal Business Association; I know the Ford Presidential Library has a copy of the final version of that speech text, though I can't find it at the moment. I want you to find that library's copy of that speech version for me, because there are some lines of poetry quoted in that speech, and I want to use them myself -- can you reply with just the title and author of the poem from which those quoted lines are taken? If the secretary misquoted the poem a bit, that's okay -- I expect that the full quote of the poem will give a very clear understanding of which poem was being referred to. Give your answer in the following form: "[TITLE], by [AUTHOR]". For example, if the poem was The Road Not Taken, written by Robert Frost, you would answer: The Road Not Taken, by Robert Frost

Title: A Pair of Poems (I): Leonard Cohen – ‘As the mist leaves no scar’ from The Spice-Box of Earth
Chunks: 0
Another mid-week pair of poems, as promised. Leonard Cohen was known primarily as a singer-songwriter, with songs such as ‘Hallelujah’ and ‘Suzanne’, but he was also an excellent poet and novelist, and it was the collection _Let Us Compare Mythologies_ (1956) that made his name as a writer in Canada, 11 years before his debut album _Songs of Leonard Cohen_(1967) was made his name as a musician. Cohen’s early collections were made up of a combination of free verse and ballad verse. Taking inspiration from European Writers such as Federico Garcia Lorca, his free verse is sparsely written, often upon sensual themes. This first collection included, for example, the following (not today’s featured poem but a lovely introduction nevertheless:
**Poem**
I heard of a man  
who says words so beautifully  
that if he only speaks their name  
women give themselves to him.
If I am dumb beside your body  
while silence blossoms like tumours on our lips  
it is because I hear a man climb stairs  
and clear his throat outside the door.  
Cohen’s second collection _The Spice-Box of Earth_(1961) featured much more poetry inspired by ballad-verse. Early musical influences start to appear, and although still relatively free of meter (at least strict meter) this second collection has far more in the way of rhyme. A master of the ABAB and -A-A quatrains, Cohen ballad verses remain sparsely written and upon sensual themes. He also starts to name poems after their opening lines, as it true of ‘As the mist leaves no scar’, and capitalises the first letter of each line, despite the punctuation (notice that this is not true of ‘Poem’). This was a common practice for the medieval and early modern ballads of British poetry, as well as some early American poetry by the likes of Henry Wadsworth Longfellow and Ralph Waldo Emerson. Here is today’s poem, the first in this week’s pair:
**As the mist leaves no scar**
As the mist leaves no scar  
On the dark green hill,  
So my body leaves no scar  
On you, nor ever will.
When wind and hawk encounter,  
What remains to keep?  
So you and I encounter,  
Then turn, then fall to sleep.
